segments.original: This film, the first blockbuster in the history of horror cinema, had an enormous influence on the future of the genre. Never before had a horror film been the object of so much attention prior to its release, so much gossip about conflicts during post-production, so much speculation about why people of all ages stood in line for hours to see a work supposedly capable of inducing fits of vomiting, fainting, and even temporary psychosis. It is hard to convey the true cultural impact of The Exorcist. The film stole headlines from the Watergate scandal, at least for a while caused a considerable rise in the number of "real" cases of demonic possession and, as one critic wrote, "established grossness as a form of mass entertainment".

segments.original: Since its inception, cinema has always flirted with the fantastic and with fear. The first horror film is called Le manoir du diable (1896) and was directed by Georges Méliès (1861-1938); already at this early stage one notices a strong influence of the fantastic and the personification of an evil figure that tends to have the upper hand over the heroes. Along with the use of a menacing villain, it also became a rule to build a setting that did nothing to make the protagonists' lives easier, as can be seen in the aforementioned Méliès work and also in the Italian film L'inferno (Dante's Inferno, 1911), whose adaptation of Dante Alighieri's journey through the circles of hell featured a set design unique for its time, making skillful use of entirely new camera shots as well as illusionism and lighting techniques.

segments.original: No director since Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980) has captured the delicious voyeurism of horror as well as John Carpenter does in Halloween, a film so full of our most primal anxieties that it still defines the genre 20 years later. Indeed, the comparison between Hitchcock and Carpenter is no exaggeration: Halloween is full of Carpenter's tributes to Hitchcock, from the characters' names - Sam Loomis and Tom Doyle, from Psycho (1960) and Rear Window (1954), respectively - to the casting of Jamie Lee Curtis (b. 1958), daughter of Janet Leigh (1927-2004), the unfortunate shower victim of Psycho.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Halloween's plot is quite simple: a masked psychopath, Michael Myers, stabs and strangles his way through a group of teenage friends as they drink beer and chase after sex, until he finally comes up against the film's great pure force, the virginal babysitter Laurie Strode (Curtis). Despite its minimalism, the evident social anxieties of good versus evil in Halloween's plot are left unresolved at the end, a strategy repeated consistently in other slashers ranging from Friday the 13th (1980) to Scream (1996). The intensity of Carpenter and of Debra Hill's (1950–2005) screenplay lies in placing horror in the placid setting of suburban American life, where young people are presumed (or at least were once presumed) to be safe.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre defined the following rules: the serial killer would keep his identity secret. His methods of murder would not be limited to simply stabbing. The victims would be mostly young people constantly using drugs or having sex (the symbolism of lost purity and the punishment represented by the killer are very strong concepts in the early drafts of the Massacre screenplay), and the location of the murders would vary between isolated spaces, such as forests and farms, or urban ones, such as houses or schools. One of the victims would always survive at the end.

segments.original: The '90s, however, held one last ace up the sleeve for the slasher when director Wes Craven (b. 1939) and screenwriter Kevin Williamson (b. 1965) teamed up and launched the Scream saga with Scream (1996). segments.original: In other words, the story would not be comedic and would carry its own suspense, but it would constantly play with the conventions of the subgenre, such as the final girl, the killer's creative methods, stylized costumes, sexual morality, and so on. For a while, the success of Scream spurred the emergence of another franchise, I Know What You Did Last Summer (1997), which, lacking any originality, failed to replicate the success of Craven and Williamson's saga. Scream can also be considered the last great example of the slasher, which, despite sporadic works, has been losing ground to another subgenre, the haunting film.
